description: .Houston team tackling Flame in Freefall: using AI + NASA microgravity combustion data to make spacecraft safer from fire. I’m Kavin, founder of PandaPCs (custom PC biz). I handle product, design, video, and the pitch. We move fast and ship real stuff. Looking for: Python/ML (pandas, scikit-learn), dashboard/front-end (Streamlit, React), and anyone into physics, chem, or aerospace.
summary:
A Moon base will run at about 30% oxygen instead of Earth's 21%, and flames behave differently without gravity. Burn Scan lets anyone photograph an item going into a habitat and see where each of its materials sits in everything NASA has burned in space.

Every NASA microgravity test of a material is placed on a chart by oxygen and pressure and marked by what happened: burned, went out, or did not ignite. Moon Base and ISS conditions are pinned on the same chart, and every point opens the paper, page and quote it came from. An atlas shows every tested material at once, and a habitat report lists what has and has not been tested for a whole room or cargo load.

It addresses the challenge by turning 13 experiments and 44 NASA papers into something a habitat designer, cargo planner or student can read in a minute. It also shows the gaps: of the 70 fuels in the papers we indexed, 67 have no recorded test at Moon Base oxygen. That tells mission planners what still needs testing.
details:
What it does

1. Scan. Take a photo, scan a care label, or type the materials. An AI vision model proposes the parts and materials, and the person confirms or corrects them before anything is looked up.

2. Flammability map. For each material, NASA's microgravity tests are placed by oxygen (%) and pressure (kPa), with a different shape and colour for each outcome. Moon Base (30% O2, 10.2 psi) and ISS (21% O2, 14.7 psi) are marked. Tapping a point shows the paper, the NASA link, the page, the quote and the outcome.

3. Atlas. Every material with NASA microgravity tests, one small map each, sortable by number of tests or by what burned at Moon Base oxygen.

4. Habitat report. Scanned items are saved on the device and grouped into spaces. The report groups a space's materials as burned in NASA tests at or above Moon Base oxygen, tested only below it, or never tested in microgravity. It lists NASA's findings under Prevention, Detection and Suppression, and prints as a report.

5. Test next. For each material, what the data does not contain, such as "no microgravity test" or "no test above 21% O2". It is worded as a gap in the data, not a verdict on the item.

6. Experiments, Papers and Ask. The 13 experiments and their papers, and a question box that answers with citations.

Benefits and intended impact

NASA's combustion data is spread across decades of technical reports, with test conditions written as free text. Burn Scan collects it in one database, stores oxygen, pressure and airflow as numbers so tests from different papers can sit on one chart, and starts from a real object instead of a search box. Habitat designers and cargo planners can see what has been tested near a habitat's atmosphere. The gap list shows where new experiments are needed.

Data

NASA core: papers from the NASA Technical Reports Server for the BASS, BASS-II, Saffire I-III, SAME, SAME-R, FLEX, FLEX-2, CFI, ACME, SPICE and SLICE experiments: 44 papers, 155 test conditions naming 70 fuels, and 231 findings.

A separate, labelled layer holds 533 published results for 99 materials from 189 documents (other NASA reports, FAA, NIST, USDA Forest Products Laboratory and peer-reviewed journals). Each row stores its link, page and exact quote. Results from Earth, weightlessness, lunar and Martian gravity are labelled and never mixed on one chart.

Tools

Site: Rust (Axum, Askama templates), plain JavaScript, Tailwind CSS. Charts are inline SVG and the flame is a WebGL shader, with no chart or 3D library. Hosted on Netlify.

Database: Postgres on Supabase, read through a read-only public key.

Backend: a separate Rust service that finds NTRS papers, extracts conditions and findings, answers questions with citations and matches material names.

It runs in a phone or laptop browser with nothing to install.

How it is creative

Most fire-safety tools start from a material name or a document. Burn Scan starts from a photo of a real object and ends on a map of real experiments, so specialist research becomes usable in about a minute. Treating "not tested" as a result, and listing it, turns the tool into a research-gap finder.

What we considered

- Nothing is fitted, predicted or averaged. A material with no test shows "no test found".

- A photo cannot prove what something is made of, so every identification is an estimate the person confirms.

- Test conditions and findings were read from the papers by an AI model. Each carries its source quote, and none has been reviewed by a person yet. The site says so wherever they are shown.

- Only 21 of 147 fuel-naming test conditions state both an oxygen level and a pressure that can be read as numbers, so most maps are sparse and say "Only N tests".

- This is research context for design, not a certification or a safety rating.
